title: Empty Pools and the First Skateparks
bigQuestion: How did empty swimming pools and new wheels lead to the first skateparks, and why did so many of those parks close?

story.title: A Wave Made of Concrete
story.kicker: In a dry summer in Southern California, a skater looks into an empty pool and sees a wave that never stops.
paragraphs: The summer is hot and dry in Southern California. A teenage skater climbs a backyard fence with a board under one arm. The family who owns the house has drained their pool. There is no water to fill it again, so it sits empty and quiet in the sun.

The skater kneels at the edge and looks down. The pool is shaped like a kidney bean. The flat floor of the deep end curves up into a smooth wall. At the top of the wall is a strip of blue tile and then a rounded stone lip. To a surfer, that curve looks like the face of a wave.

The skater climbs down the steps in the shallow end. They push off and roll toward the deep end. The board picks up speed on the slope. At the bottom, the wall rises ahead. They lean, carve up the curve, and feel the wheels grip the concrete. Near the tile the board slows, turns, and rolls back down.

Each run climbs a little higher. Soon the wheels are almost touching the tile. The skater is riding a wave made of concrete, and it never breaks. Across the region, other skaters are finding empty pools too. What they learn in those pools will soon be poured into the first skateparks.
story.think: Why would a surfer look at the curved wall of an empty pool and think of a wave?

lessons.title: Backyard Pools in California
lessons.mainIdea: In the 1970s, skaters in Southern California rode empty backyard pools because their smooth curved walls felt like waves.
reading: Southern California has many backyard swimming pools. Many were built after World War II, when the area grew fast. Pools from that time often had rounded shapes, like a kidney bean or a figure eight. Their floors curved smoothly up into the walls. That curve is what drew skaters.

Some skaters were riding empty pools even before the 1970s. Then came the *drought* of 1976 and 1977. A drought is a long time with much less rain than normal. Water was scarce, so some owners drained their pools or left them empty. Skaters went looking for them. They called this *pool riding*.

Many of these skaters were surfers first. The Zephyr team from Santa Monica and Venice had shown a low, surf-style way to skate at the Del Mar Nationals in 1975. Its riders included Peggy Oki, Tony Alva, Jay Adams and Stacy Peralta. In pools, that style could climb walls. Skating an empty pool without the owner's permission was trespassing, and that is part of this history too.

words.d: a long period with much less rain than normal
skateboarding in an empty swimming pool, using its curved walls like a wave
going onto someone else's property without permission

look.title: Two Pools Side by Side
look.text: Picture two empty pools. The first is a rectangle with a flat floor and straight walls that meet the floor at a sharp corner. The second is shaped like a kidney bean, and its floor bends in a smooth curve up into the wall. Roll a ball toward each wall. In the first pool, the ball hits the corner and bounces back. In the second, the ball rolls up the curve and back down.
look.prompt: Which pool would a skater choose, and what about its shape makes the difference?

check.q: What is a drought?
choices: a long period with much less rain than normal
a deep end of a swimming pool
a contest held in a pool
check.why: A drought is a long dry period. The drought of 1976 and 1977 left many California pools empty.

check.q: Why did rounded backyard pools work well for skating?
choices: They had sharp corners to bounce off
They were always full of water
Their floors curved smoothly up into the walls
check.why: A rounded pool's floor bends into its wall, so a board can roll up the curve like a wave.

check.q: Which group showed a low, surf-style way of skating at the Del Mar Nationals in 1975?
check.why: The Zephyr team from Santa Monica and Venice skated at Del Mar in 1975. The Bones Brigade came later.

lessons.title: The Parts of a Pool
lessons.mainIdea: Skaters learned names for each part of a pool: the flat bottom, the curved transition, the vertical wall, the tile and the coping.
reading: A pool gave skaters a new set of words. The flat floor at the bottom is the *flat bottom*. The curved part where the floor bends up into the wall is the *transition*, often called tranny for short. Above the transition, the wall can become straight up and down. Skaters call that part *vert*, short for vertical.

At the top of a pool wall is a band of tile. Above the tile is the *coping*. In a pool, coping is the rounded stone or concrete lip along the edge. Skaters learned to ride up until their wheels touched the tile. Later they rolled their back truck onto the coping and let it grind along the edge.

Pools also have a shallow end and a deep end. The deep end has the tallest walls, so it is where the biggest moves happen. The shallow end often has steps. Skaters used the steps to climb in and out. These same words, from transition to coping, are still used in every skatepark today.

words.d: the curved part of a ramp or pool where the flat floor bends up into the wall
short for vertical; the part of a wall that goes straight up and down
the rounded lip along the top edge of a pool or ramp
the flat floor at the bottom of a pool or ramp

look.title: A Pool Wall From the Side
look.text: Imagine cutting a pool in half and looking at the deep end from the side. At the bottom is a flat line: the flat bottom. Then the line bends upward in a smooth curve: the transition. Near the top, the curve stands straight up for a short way: the vert. Last comes a strip of tile and, on top, a rounded lip: the coping.
look.prompt: Trace the wall with your finger from the floor to the top. Name each part as you pass it.

check.q: What is the transition?
choices: the straight-up part at the top of a wall
the curved part where the floor bends up into the wall
the rounded lip on the edge
the steps in the shallow end
check.why: The transition is the curve between the flat floor and the wall.

check.q: In a pool, what is the coping?
choices: the drain in the deep end
the rounded stone or concrete lip along the top edge
the band of tile below the edge
check.why: Coping is the rounded lip at the very top of the wall, above the tile.

check.q: Why did the biggest moves happen in the deep end?
choices: It is where the water stays
check.why: The deep end has the tallest walls, so skaters can ride higher there.

lessons.title: Wheels and Bearings That Grip
lessons.mainIdea: Urethane wheels and sealed precision bearings made it possible to grip a curved wall and roll smoothly up it.
reading: In the 1960s, most skateboard wheels were made of clay or metal. They were hard and slippery. On a curved wall, they would skid out. In the early 1970s, Frank Nasworthy began selling wheels made of *urethane*, a tough, rubbery plastic. His company was called Cadillac Wheels.

Urethane wheels grip the ground much better than clay. They also roll over small cracks and pebbles instead of stopping short. That grip comes from *friction*, the force that pushes against sliding between two surfaces. With more grip, a skater could lean into a turn on a steep wall and the wheels would hold.

In the mid-1970s, sealed precision bearings came to skateboards. A bearing is a ring of small steel balls inside each wheel that lets the wheel spin smoothly on the axle. Sealed bearings kept out dirt and rolled with less loss. Together, grippy wheels and smooth bearings let skaters carry speed up the walls of a pool.

words.d: a tough, rubbery plastic used for skateboard wheels since the early 1970s
a force that pushes against sliding between two surfaces that touch
a ring of small steel balls inside a wheel that lets it spin smoothly on the axle

look.title: Clay Wheel, Urethane Wheel
look.text: Picture two boards rolling toward the same curved wall. The first has hard clay wheels. As it starts up the curve and the rider leans, the wheels skid sideways and the board slips out. The second has urethane wheels. As it leans on the same curve, the wheels hold the concrete and the board keeps climbing.
look.prompt: Which force is stronger for the urethane wheels, and how does that help the rider?

check.q: Who began selling urethane skateboard wheels in the early 1970s?
check.why: Frank Nasworthy sold urethane wheels through his company, Cadillac Wheels.

check.q: Why did urethane wheels work better on a curved wall than clay wheels?
choices: They are harder and more slippery
They grip the concrete with more friction
check.why: Urethane grips better, so the wheels hold when the rider leans on a steep curve.

check.q: What does a bearing do?
choices: holds the grip tape on the deck
connects the trucks to the deck
lets the wheel spin smoothly on the axle
makes the wheel grip the ground
check.why: A bearing is a ring of small steel balls that lets the wheel spin smoothly.

sections.title: Up the Wall and Into the Air

lessons.title: Riding the Curve
lessons.mainIdea: On a curved transition, the wall pushes the skater around the curve, so the skater feels heavier at the bottom.
reading: When a skater rolls into the curve of a pool, their path bends upward. Anything that moves in a curve needs a push toward the center of that curve. Here, the wall gives that push. It presses up on the wheels, which press on the rider's feet. This pull toward the center is called *centripetal acceleration*.

Scientists find centripetal acceleration with a = v squared divided by r. Here v is speed and r is the *radius*, the distance from the center of the curve to the path. Here is a worked example. A skater moves at 6 meters per second through a curve with a 3-meter radius. First, 6 times 6 is 36. Next, 36 divided by 3 is 12. The answer is 12 meters per second squared.

Gravity pulls down at 9.8 meters per second squared. At the bottom of the curve, the floor must hold the rider up and also turn them. So the push adds up to 9.8 plus 12, or 21.8. That is about 2.2 times what the rider feels standing still. This is why pool skaters crouch low with bent knees at the bottom of a wall.

words.d: the change in direction of something moving in a curve, always pointed toward the center of the curve
the distance from the center of a circle or curve to its edge

look.title: Faster Means a Harder Push
look.cite: Worked example using a = v² ÷ r
look.prompt: When the speed doubles from 4 to 8 meters per second, about how many times bigger does the push get?

check.q: What gives a skater the push that turns them around the curve of a pool?
choices: the wall pressing up on the wheels
check.why: The curved wall presses on the wheels and turns the skater's path upward.

check.q: A skater moves at 4 meters per second through a curve with a 2-meter radius. What is the centripetal acceleration?
check.why: 4 times 4 is 16, and 16 divided by 2 is 8 meters per second squared.

check.q: Why do pool skaters crouch at the bottom of a wall?
choices: They feel lighter there and might float
They feel heavier there, and bent knees help them hold it
check.why: At the bottom of the curve the floor pushes harder, so the rider feels heavier and bends to handle it.

lessons.title: Speed From Height
lessons.mainIdea: Starting higher on a wall gives a skater more stored energy, which becomes more speed at the bottom.
reading: A skater at the top of a pool wall is high above the floor. Height stores energy, called *potential energy*. When the skater rolls down, that energy turns into *kinetic energy*, the energy of motion. The higher the start, the faster the skater moves at the bottom. Mass does not change the answer, so a small skater and a large skater reach about the same speed.

If nothing slowed the skater, the speed at the bottom would be v = the square root of 2 times g times h. Here g is 9.8 meters per second squared and h is the height. Here is a worked example for a 2-meter wall. First, 2 times 9.8 is 19.6. Next, 19.6 times 2 is 39.2. The square root of 39.2 is about 6.3. So the speed is about 6.3 meters per second.

Real skaters go a little slower. Friction in the wheels and bearings, and air pushing back, turn some energy into heat and sound. That is why a skater who just rolls back and forth climbs a little lower each time. To keep going, pool skaters learned to pump: crouching on the way into the curve and standing taller on the way up the wall adds energy.

words.d: stored energy that something has because of its height
the energy something has because it is moving
to crouch and stand at the right moments on a ramp to gain speed without pushing

look.title: Wall Height and Speed at the Bottom
look.unit: meters per second, with no friction
look.cite: Worked example using v = √(2gh) with g = 9.8 m/s²
look.prompt: The 4-meter wall is four times as tall as the 1-meter wall. Is the speed four times as fast? About how many times faster is it?

check.q: What kind of energy does a skater have at the top of a pool wall before rolling down?
check.why: Height stores potential energy. It becomes kinetic energy as the skater rolls down.

check.q: With no friction, about how fast is a skater moving after rolling down a 2-meter wall?
check.why: 2 times 9.8 times 2 is 39.2, and its square root is about 6.3 meters per second.

check.q: Why does a skater who only rolls back and forth climb a little lower each time?
choices: Friction and air turn some energy into heat and sound
Kinetic energy turns into more height
check.why: Some energy is lost to friction and air each trip, so the skater cannot reach the starting height.

lessons.title: The Frontside Air
lessons.mainIdea: In the late 1970s, pool skaters learned to fly above the coping by grabbing the board, an early trick called the frontside air.
reading: As wheels and walls improved, skaters rode higher and higher. In the late 1970s, some began to fly past the coping and come back down onto the wall. This is called an *air*. To keep the board with them, they grabbed it with one hand. Who did the first one is argued. Tony Alva is often named among the first, and other skaters were trying airs too.

Skaters describe turns as frontside or backside. Skaters call it *frontside* when the skater's chest and toes face the wall as they turn. It is *backside* when their back faces the wall. In a frontside air, the skater rides up the wall facing it, reaches down with the back hand, and grabs the toe-side edge of the board. Then the skater turns in the air and lands going back down the wall.

Physics explains the height. Say a skater leaves the coping moving straight up at 3 meters per second. The rise is v squared divided by 2g. First, 3 times 3 is 9. Next, 2 times 9.8 is 19.6. Then, 9 divided by 19.6 is about 0.46. The skater rises about 0.46 meters above the coping. Airs like this are for experienced riders in a skatepark, after years of smaller steps.

words.d: a trick where the skater and board leave the ramp or wall and fly before landing again
a turn or trick where the skater's chest and toes face the wall or obstacle
a turn or trick where the skater's back faces the wall or obstacle

look.title: A Frontside Air, Frame by Frame
look.text: Frame 1: the skater rolls up the deep-end wall, facing it, knees bent. Frame 2: the wheels reach the coping, and the back hand reaches down to the toe-side edge. Frame 3: skater and board rise together above the coping, turning in the air. Frame 4: the turn finishes, and the wheels meet the wall again, rolling down. Frame 5: the skater crouches low through the transition.
look.prompt: In which frame is the skater moving slowest? Explain using what gravity does on the way up.

check.q: What does frontside mean?
choices: the skater's chest and toes face the wall as they turn
the skater's back faces the wall as they turn
the skater rides with the front foot on the tail
the skater rides in the shallow end
check.why: Frontside means the front of the body faces the wall or obstacle.

check.q: In a frontside air, which hand grabs the board, and where?
choices: the back hand grabs the toe-side edge
the front hand grabs the nose
the back hand grabs the heel-side edge
check.why: In a frontside air the back hand reaches down to the toe-side edge.

check.q: A skater leaves the coping moving straight up at 3 meters per second. About how high above the coping do they rise?
check.why: 3 times 3 is 9, and 9 divided by 19.6 is about 0.46 meters.

lessons.title: 1976: Carlsbad and Port Orange
lessons.mainIdea: Two of the first built skateparks, Carlsbad Skatepark in California and Skateboard City in Florida, opened in 1976.
reading: Pools were hard to find, and skating them often meant trespassing. Business owners saw a chance. Why not build places made just for skating? A *skatepark* is a place built for skateboarding, with ramps, bowls and curves. In 1976, two of the first opened on opposite coasts of the United States.

Carlsbad Skatepark opened in Carlsbad, California, north of San Diego. Skateboard City opened in Port Orange, Florida, near Daytona Beach. Both were built of poured concrete. Which one opened first is argued, so it is safest to say both opened in 1976. Florida also had warm weather all year and a strong surfing culture, like California.

Early parks copied what skaters loved about pools. Builders shaped concrete into *bowls*, deep rounded holes with curved walls. Some parks also had snake runs. A snake run is a long, winding downhill channel with curved banks, a bit like a dry riverbed. For the first time, skaters could ride curves legally and without hunting for an empty pool.

words.d: a place built for skateboarding, with ramps, bowls and curves
deep rounded holes in a skatepark with curved walls, shaped like pools
a long, winding downhill channel with curved banks for skating

look.title: From Wheels to Parks
rows: Del Mar Nationals with the Zephyr team
look.cite: Dates as commonly given in skateboarding histories
look.prompt: How many years passed between the kicktail patent and the first parks?

check.q: In what year did Carlsbad Skatepark and Skateboard City both open?
check.why: Both of these early concrete skateparks opened in 1976.

check.q: Where was Skateboard City?
check.why: Skateboard City opened in Port Orange, Florida, near Daytona Beach.

check.q: What is a snake run?
choices: a deep round bowl shaped like a pool
a long, winding downhill channel with curved banks
a wooden ramp in a backyard
check.why: A snake run winds downhill with curved banks, a bit like a dry riverbed.

lessons.title: The Park Boom
lessons.mainIdea: By the late 1970s, dozens of paid skateparks had opened across the United States, often with rules about helmets and pads.
reading: After 1976, skateparks spread quickly. By the late 1970s, dozens had opened across the United States, and parks appeared in other countries too. This fast growth is called a *boom*. It was skateboarding's second boom, after the first one in the early 1960s faded around 1965 and 1966.

Most of these parks were private businesses. Skaters paid to ride, often for a *session*, a set block of time. Many parks had rules that riders wear a helmet and pads. Some rented gear at the front desk. Parks often held contests, and local skaters could watch better riders up close and learn from them.

Parks changed how skaters learned. A beginner could practice on a small, gentle bank before trying a tall bowl. A good progression starts small, with a helmet buckled and pads on, and moves up only when the smaller step feels easy. That idea, start low and build up, began in those first parks and still guides every skatepark today.

words.d: a time of fast growth, when many more people take part and buy products
a set block of time for skating; also a group of skaters riding together
learning in steps, from easy and low to harder and higher

look.title: A Day at a 1970s Park
look.text: A skater pays at a window and gets a wristband for a two-hour session. A sign says helmets and pads are required. Inside, a small bank sits near the entrance, a snake run winds downhill, and a deep bowl waits at the back. Beginners practice turns on the bank. Older riders carve the bowl, and a crowd gathers at its edge to watch.
look.prompt: Where in this park would you start, and what would make you ready to move to the next area?

check.q: What was a session at a 1970s skatepark?
choices: a set block of time that skaters paid to ride
a kind of trick in the air
the deepest bowl in the park
check.why: Many parks charged skaters for a session, a set block of time.

check.q: Which boom was the skatepark boom of the late 1970s?
check.why: The first boom faded around 1965 and 1966. The park boom of the 1970s was the second.

check.q: What does a good progression look like?
choices: start in the deepest bowl to learn fast
skip the helmet on small banks
start low and small with gear, and move up when that step feels easy
check.why: A progression builds from easy and low to harder and higher, with gear on.

lessons.title: SkateBoarder Magazine
lessons.mainIdea: SkateBoarder magazine spread pool and park skating across the country through photos and stories in the 1970s.
reading: Before the internet, most skaters learned about new tricks from *magazines*. The most important one in the 1970s was SkateBoarder. It first appeared in the 1960s, stopped when the first boom faded, and came back in the mid-1970s. Each issue had big color photos of skaters in pools and parks.

Photos showed what words could not. A picture of a skater high on a pool wall told a kid in another state that it could be done. Writer and artist Craig Stecyk wrote about the Santa Monica and Venice skaters, an area called *Dogtown*. Those stories helped make Zephyr riders famous far from California.

Magazines also ran ads for boards, wheels and parks. Companies paid skaters to ride their products. These skaters were called *pros*, short for professionals. A young skater who wanted to see the newest tricks waited each month for the next issue to arrive.

words.d: printed publications with photos and stories that come out on a schedule, such as every month
a nickname for parts of Santa Monica and Venice, California, where the Zephyr skaters rode
short for professionals; skaters paid to ride for a company

look.title: A Photo Travels
look.text: A photographer kneels at the edge of a deep pool in California. Click: a skater hangs at the top of the wall, wheels just below the tile. Weeks later, that photo is printed across two pages of a magazine. A kid far from the coast opens the magazine and stares at it for a long time. The next day, the kid draws a pool wall in a notebook.
look.prompt: How did one photo change what a skater far away believed was possible?

check.q: What was the most important skateboarding magazine of the 1970s?
check.why: SkateBoarder led in the 1970s. Thrasher began in 1981 and TransWorld in 1983.

check.q: What was Dogtown?
choices: a nickname for parts of Santa Monica and Venice where the Zephyr skaters rode
check.why: Dogtown was a nickname for an area of Santa Monica and Venice, written about by Craig Stecyk.

check.q: What is a pro skater?
choices: a skater paid to ride for a company
a skater who only rides pools
check.why: Pro is short for professional, a skater who is paid to ride a company's products.

lessons.title: Insurance and Lawsuits
lessons.mainIdea: In the early 1980s, high insurance costs and injury lawsuits closed many skateparks.
reading: Skaters fall, and sometimes they get hurt. When someone was hurt at a park, they or their family could sue the owner. A *lawsuit* is a case taken to court to ask for money for a harm. Even a park that won in court had to pay lawyers. Each lawsuit raised the risk of running a park.

Park owners bought *insurance*. Insurance is a plan where you pay a company regularly, and it pays big costs if something goes wrong. As claims grew, insurance companies charged park owners more, or refused to cover them. For many owners, the cost became more than the park earned.

Many parks closed in the early 1980s. Some were torn down. Others were filled with dirt and buried. At the same time, fewer people were buying skateboards, so parks had fewer paying riders. Losing the parks was a blow, but skaters did not stop. They found other places to ride.

words.d: a case taken to court in which someone asks for money for a harm
a plan where you pay a company regularly and it pays large costs if something goes wrong

look.title: A Park Owner's Math
look.text: Picture the money for one park as two piles. Pile one is money coming in: session fees, gear rentals and snacks. Pile two is money going out: workers, repairs, electric bills and insurance. One year the insurance bill doubles. Pile two grows taller than pile one. Then fewer skaters come, and pile one shrinks.
look.prompt: What choices does the owner have when the money going out is bigger than the money coming in?

check.q: What closed many skateparks in the early 1980s?
choices: the start of the X Games
high insurance costs and injury lawsuits
check.why: Rising insurance costs and lawsuits made many parks too expensive to run.

check.q: What is insurance?
choices: a rule that skaters must wear pads
a plan where you pay a company and it pays big costs if something goes wrong
check.why: Insurance spreads risk: you pay regularly, and the company pays large costs.

check.q: Besides insurance, what else made parks harder to keep open?
choices: fewer people were buying skateboards, so fewer riders came
check.why: Skateboard sales fell at the same time, so parks earned less.

lessons.title: What Skaters Did Next
lessons.mainIdea: When parks closed, skaters built wooden ramps and took to the streets, and later public parks returned.
reading: With parks closing, skaters built their own places. Many built *halfpipes* out of wood in backyards. A halfpipe is a U-shaped ramp with two curved walls facing each other. Plywood bent over wooden frames made a smooth transition. Friends pooled money for lumber and built them together.

Other skaters rode what the city already had: curbs, banks, benches and empty parking lots. This became *street skating*, which grew in the 1980s. It needed new tricks, and the ollie on flat ground would soon give skaters a way to get up onto things without ramps.

Skateparks came back, but in a new form. Over time, more cities built *public* parks, owned by the town and often free to use. Some states changed their laws to protect cities from many lawsuits when skaters at public parks are hurt. Today a good first visit still means a helmet that fits and is buckled, wrist guards and pads, and starting on the smallest bank.

words.d: U-shaped ramps with two curved walls facing each other
skating on things found in a town, such as curbs, ledges and banks
owned by a town or city and open to everyone

look.title: Wrist Guards Matter
look.text: Wrist injuries are among the most common skateboarding injuries. Wearing wrist guards, along with a helmet and knee and elbow pads, helps prevent many of them.
look.cite: U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission, skateboarding safety guidance
look.prompt: Why might wrist injuries be so common when a skater falls? What does a wrist guard do?

check.why: A halfpipe has two curved walls facing each other, like a U.

check.q: What is street skating?
